triage.name: Fever
triage.reason: Core undifferentiated symptom with a wide differential (infection, inflammatory, malignant, drug) that students must reason through with history, exam and cultures.

age.peak: bimodal: children under 5 and adults over 65

demographics: Occurs at all ages; young children and older adults are most vulnerable to infection-related fever
More frequent in people with chronic illness, recent hospitalization, or immunosuppression

risk_factors.text: Recent or current infection (respiratory, urinary, gastrointestinal, skin)
Recent hospitalization, surgery, or indwelling devices (catheters, lines)
Very young or very old age
Recent travel or exposure to sick contacts
Use of medications that can cause drug fever

hpi.onset: Sudden or gradual depending on cause; often noticed over hours to a day
hpi.duration: Variable; acute infections typically cause fever for a few days, while chronic causes may last weeks
hpi.progression: May spike and fall (intermittent) or remain persistently elevated; pattern depends on the underlying cause
hpi.quality: Subjective feeling of heat, often with chills or shivering
hpi.severity: Mild to high; temperature often 100.4–104 °F (38–40 °C), can be higher
hpi.timing: Can be continuous, intermittent, or remittent
pertinent_negatives: No confusion or altered mental status
No focal pain localizing to a specific organ

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants may not mount a fever or may present with nonspecific signs like poor feeding, irritability, lethargy, or temperature instability.
Older adults may have a blunted fever response, and fever may be absent or low-grade despite serious infection; they may present with confusion or falls.
Immunocompromised patients may have minimal or no fever despite severe infection, or fever may be the only sign.
Baseline body temperature is slightly higher in pregnancy; fever may be blunted or attributed to other causes, and some infections pose fetal risk.

general.mild: Alert, mildly flushed, comfortable at rest, no distress
general.moderate: Flushed and warm, appears uncomfortable, prefers to lie still
general.severe: Ill-appearing, diaphoretic, shivering or rigoring, tachycardic
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, mottled or pale, may be hypotensive

findings.maneuver: Measure the temperature (oral, tympanic, temporal, axillary, or rectal)
findings.finding: Body temperature above the normal range (generally >100.4 °F / 38 °C)

findings.maneuver: Palpate the skin of the trunk and extremities
findings.finding: Skin feels warm or hot to the touch

findings.maneuver: Palpate the radial pulse or auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Heart rate elevated above the expected rate for the temperature

findings.maneuver: Observe and count the respiratory rate

findings.finding: Low blood pressure, suggesting sepsis or shock

findings.maneuver: Assess orientation, attention, and level of consciousness
Flex the neck and assess for resistance
Palpate the abdomen and other regions for focal tenderness
findings.finding: No focal tenderness or mass localizing to a specific organ

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph node chains
findings.finding: No enlarged or tender lymph nodes
Clear breath sounds without crackles or consolidation

labs.caveat: A normal or low white count does not exclude serious infection; leukopenia can occur in overwhelming sepsis or viral illness.
A left shift supports bacterial infection but is nonspecific.
Thrombocytopenia suggests severe sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, or a hematologic process.
Nonspecific; helps gauge the magnitude of inflammation but does not identify the source.
Rises and falls slowly; more useful for chronic or inflammatory causes than acute infection.
Higher values favor bacterial infection and sepsis; normal values do not fully exclude it.
Elevated lactate with fever suggests hypoperfusion or sepsis and should prompt urgent evaluation.
Rises with dehydration from fever, poor intake, or vomiting.
Elevated creatinine suggests dehydration or renal injury from sepsis.
Hyponatremia can accompany pneumonia, meningitis, or other infections.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic acidosis, which may accompany sepsis or dehydration.
Hyperglycemia can be stress-related or indicate undiagnosed diabetes; infection worsens glycemic control.
Positive leukocyte esterase supports urinary tract infection as the fever source.
Positive nitrite is fairly specific for a Gram-negative urinary infection.
Pyuria supports urinary infection but can also occur with sterile inflammation.
Only obtained when meningitis or encephalitis is suspected; elevated counts with neutrophil predominance suggest bacterial meningitis.
Low CSF glucose relative to serum favors bacterial or fungal meningitis.
Check in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy.

findings.finding: Sinus tachycardia, roughly 10 beats per minute above normal for each 1 °F of fever
Sinus rhythm; irregularly irregular rhythm suggests atrial fibrillation, which can be triggered by infection or sepsis
Relative bradycardia (heart rate not rising as expected with fever), which can point to typhoid fever, Legionella, or a drug effect
Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression suggesting acute pericarditis
Peaked T waves suggesting hyperkalemia in the setting of sepsis or renal failure

imaging.preferred_when: First-line when pneumonia or another chest source is suspected

findings.text: Lobar or segmental consolidation with air bronchograms

imaging.preferred_when: When chest x-ray is nondiagnostic or a complicated pulmonary infection is suspected

findings.text: Consolidation, ground-glass opacities, or tree-in-bud nodularity

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Fever with abdominal pain, tenderness, or an unclear source

findings.text: Focal inflammatory change or abscess in an abdominal organ
Bowel wall thickening or pericolonic stranding
Free fluid or free air suggesting perforation

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the abdomen, right upper quadrant
imaging.preferred_when: Fever with right upper quadrant pain or abnormal liver tests; preferred in pregnancy and children

findings.text: Gallstones or gallbladder wall thickening suggesting cholecystitis
Biliary duct dilation suggesting obstruction or cholangitis

imaging.preferred_when: Fever with altered mental status or new focal neurologic deficit before lumbar puncture

findings.text: Cerebral edema, mass, or hydrocephalus that would make lumbar puncture unsafe
Sinusitis or mastoiditis as a source of fever

imaging.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected encephalitis or brain abscess when CT is nondiagnostic

findings.text: Temporal lobe signal abnormality suggesting herpes encephalitis

imaging.study: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
imaging.preferred_when: Fever with flank pain, urinary symptoms, or suspected obstruction; avoids radiation in pregnancy

initial.why: White count and differential help distinguish bacterial from viral illness and detect leukopenia or thrombocytopenia
Assesses hydration, renal function, electrolytes, and acidosis in a febrile patient
Urinary tract infection is a common and easily missed source of fever
Identifies bacteremia and guides antibiotics in moderate to severe fever
Looks for pneumonia when respiratory symptoms or abnormal lung exam are present
initial.only_if: respiratory symptoms, abnormal lung exam, or no clear source

initial.why: Rules out pregnancy before imaging or medication choices
Confirms influenza when it would change antiviral treatment
initial.only_if: influenza is circulating and symptoms are compatible

confirmatory.why: Confirms urinary tract infection when urinalysis is abnormal or symptoms are present
Identifies the pathogen in suspected bacterial pneumonia
confirmatory.only_if: productive cough or an infiltrate on chest imaging

confirmatory.why: Confirms bacterial meningitis when lumbar puncture is performed

confirmatory.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Identifies an intra-abdominal abscess or other source when the history and exam point to the abdomen
confirmatory.only_if: abdominal pain, tenderness, or an unexplained fever

supporting.why: Supports the presence and magnitude of inflammation
Adds evidence of inflammation, especially in subacute or chronic fever
Favors bacterial infection and can support antibiotic decisions
Defines a pulmonary source when chest x-ray is nondiagnostic
supporting.only_if: chest x-ray is inconclusive or a complicated infection is suspected

supporting.test: Ultrasound of the abdomen, right upper quadrant
supporting.why: Evaluates for cholecystitis or biliary obstruction
supporting.only_if: right upper quadrant pain or abnormal liver tests

supporting.why: Rules out a mass or raised pressure before lumbar puncture
supporting.only_if: altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit

supporting.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
supporting.only_if: suspected encephalitis or a focal brain lesion

supporting.test: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
supporting.only_if: flank pain or suspected urinary obstruction

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine for fever without abdominal findings
not_indicated.only_if: abdominal pain, tenderness, or an unexplained fever

not_indicated.why: Not needed when chest x-ray is adequate
not_indicated.only_if: chest x-ray is inconclusive or a complicated infection is suspected
altered mental status or focal neurologic deficit

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Reserved for suspected encephalitis or abscess
not_indicated.only_if: suspected encephalitis or a focal brain lesion

not_indicated.test: Ultrasound of the abdomen, right upper quadrant
not_indicated.why: Not routine without right upper quadrant symptoms or abnormal liver tests
not_indicated.only_if: right upper quadrant pain or abnormal liver tests

not_indicated.test: Ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
not_indicated.why: Not routine without urinary or flank symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: flank pain or suspected urinary obstruction

not_indicated.why: Nonspecific and not useful for identifying the source of fever
Not part of the acute fever workup unless thyroid disease is suspected
Not needed unless the pain is epigastric or pancreatitis is suspected
Not routine outside influenza season or without compatible symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: influenza is circulating and symptoms are compatible

decision_points: Check pregnancy status before imaging or medications that are unsafe in pregnancy
Obtain blood cultures before starting antibiotics whenever possible
Lactate and blood cultures promptly in any patient who appears septic or hypotensive
Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture in suspected bacterial meningitis; draw cultures and start treatment first
Consider drug fever when the fever persists without a source and the medication list includes a likely culprit

differential.name: Bacterial sepsis
differential.why_considered: Fever is the most common presenting sign of a bloodstream or systemic bacterial infection, and it can be the only early clue.
differential.trigger: Fever with tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status, or rigors

history: Recent infection, surgery, or indwelling device
exam: Focal source on exam (lungs, urine, skin, abdomen)
labs: Leukocytosis with a left shift or leukopenia
imaging: Chest x-ray or CT showing a source such as pneumonia or an abscess

differential.name: Pneumonia
differential.why_considered: A common and easily missed source of fever, especially in older adults who may not report cough.

history: Productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, shortness of breath
Older age or chronic lung disease
exam: Crackles, egophony, or dullness to percussion
labs: Positive sputum culture or blood culture
imaging: Lobar or segmental consolidation on chest x-ray
Ground-glass or consolidative opacities on CT

differential.name: Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis
differential.why_considered: A frequent source of fever, particularly in women, older adults, and patients with catheters.

exam: Confusion in older adults without localizing symptoms
labs: Pyuria, positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrite
imaging: Hydronephrosis or perinephric abscess on ultrasound or CT if obstruction is suspected

differential.name: Bacterial meningitis
differential.why_considered: Fever with headache and neck stiffness is a classic presentation that can rapidly become life-threatening.
differential.trigger: Fever with headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, or altered mental status

exam: Nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign
Altered mental status, focal neurologic deficit
labs: Elevated CSF protein, low CSF glucose
Positive CSF Gram stain or culture
imaging: CT head before lumbar puncture if altered mental status or focal deficit

differential.name: Influenza and other viral respiratory infections
differential.why_considered: A very common cause of acute fever with myalgias and respiratory symptoms, especially in season.

history: Abrupt onset of fever, myalgias, headache, sore throat
labs: Positive rapid influenza or respiratory viral panel
imaging: Normal chest x-ray unless complicated by pneumonia

differential.name: Drug fever
differential.why_considered: Fever can be the only manifestation of an adverse drug reaction and is easily overlooked when an infection has been excluded.

history: New medication started days to weeks before fever
labs: Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers

differential.name: Autoimmune or inflammatory disease
differential.why_considered: Fever is a common feature of systemic inflammatory diseases and can mimic infection.

history: Weeks to months of fever, joint pain, rash, oral ulcers
imaging: Serositis or pericardial effusion on echocardiography or CT

differential.name: Malignancy (lymphoma, leukemia)
differential.why_considered: Fever can be a presenting symptom of hematologic malignancy, often with night sweats and weight loss.
differential.trigger: Fever with night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly

history: B symptoms: fever, drenching night sweats, unintentional weight loss
labs: Cytopenias, lymphocytosis, or blasts on smear

severity.mild: Low-grade fever (99.5–100.9 °F), alert and comfortable, no focal symptoms, able to eat and drink
severity.moderate: Fever 100.4–102.2 °F with chills, malaise, tachycardia, and mild dehydration but stable vital signs
severity.severe: High fever 102–104 °F with rigors, tachypnea, hypoxemia, or focal findings suggesting a serious source
severity.critical: Fever with hypotension, altered mental status, or lactate elevation indicating sepsis or septic shock

red_flags.finding: Hypotension or systolic blood pressure below 90 mmHg
red_flags.meaning: Septic shock; requires immediate fluids, cultures, and antibiotics
Possible meningitis, encephalitis, or sepsis; urgent workup
Meningitis until proven otherwise; do not delay antibiotics
Pneumonia or sepsis with respiratory compromise
Neutropenic fever; emergency requiring broad-spectrum antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Fever lasting more than 3 weeks without a source
red_flags.meaning: Fever of unknown origin; evaluate for malignancy, autoimmune disease, or occult infection

complications.name: Febrile neutropenia
clues: Fever may be the only sign

special_populations.differences: Infants under 3 months with fever require urgent evaluation including blood, urine, and CSF cultures because signs of serious infection are nonspecific.
Fever may be blunted or absent; confusion, falls, or functional decline may be the only clue to serious infection.
Fever may be the only sign of infection; neutropenic fever is an emergency requiring immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Baseline temperature is slightly higher; fever may be blunted, and certain infections pose fetal risk. Avoid NSAIDs and tetracyclines.
Febrile seizures can occur; avoid aspirin due to Reye syndrome; use weight-based acetaminophen or ibuprofen dosing.

key_questions.question: How high has the temperature been, and how did you measure it?
key_questions.looking_for: Objective measurement above 100.4 °F (38 °C); route and reliability of measurement

key_questions.question: When did the fever start, and has it been continuous or coming and going?
key_questions.looking_for: Duration and pattern (continuous, intermittent, remittent) that narrows the cause

key_questions.question: Have you had shaking chills or drenching night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Rigors suggest bacteremia or serious infection; night sweats suggest TB, lymphoma, or endocarditis

key_questions.question: What other symptoms came with the fever — cough, sore throat, burning with urination, diarrhea, headache, rash, or joint pain?
key_questions.looking_for: A localizing symptom that points to the source

key_questions.question: Have you recently been in the hospital, had surgery, or do you have a catheter, line, or other device?
Do you take any medications that suppress the immune system, such as chemotherapy, steroids, or drugs for transplant or autoimmune disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunosuppression, which raises the risk of serious infection and blunts fever

key_questions.question: Have you started any new medication in the days to weeks before the fever began?
key_questions.looking_for: Drug fever as a cause when no infection is found

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently, or been around anyone who is sick?
Have you had any animal contact or occupational exposure?
key_questions.looking_for: Zoonotic infection such as brucellosis or leptospirosis

key_questions.question: Have you had any unintentional weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic illness such as malignancy, TB, or autoimmune disease

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which affects the differential and the safety of imaging and medications

key_questions.question: Do you have any confusion, a stiff neck, or sensitivity to light?
key_questions.looking_for: Meningitis or encephalitis, which requires urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Do you have any trouble breathing, chest pain, or a racing heart?
key_questions.looking_for: Pneumonia or sepsis with respiratory or circulatory compromise

key_questions.question: Have you fainted, felt dizzy on standing, or noticed your skin becoming mottled or clammy?
Do you have any condition or medication that affects your immune system, such as HIV, cancer, or a transplant?
key_questions.looking_for: Immunocompromised state, where fever may be the only sign of serious infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent vaccination?
key_questions.looking_for: Post-vaccination fever, which is usually mild and self-limited

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have an autoimmune disease or a history of recurrent fevers?

reasoning_points: Fever is a sign, not a diagnosis; the goal is to identify the underlying cause
Onset, duration, and pattern of the fever help narrow the differential
Associated localizing symptoms point to a specific source such as respiratory, urinary, gastrointestinal, or skin
Rigors, hypotension, altered mental status, or tachypnea suggest serious infection or sepsis
Immunosuppression, recent hospitalization, or indwelling devices raise the risk of serious infection
A new medication can cause drug fever when no infection is found
Night sweats and weight loss raise concern for malignancy, tuberculosis, or chronic infection
Pregnancy status must be checked before imaging or medication choices
Vital signs and a focused exam guide the urgency and the workup
Cultures should be obtained before antibiotics when possible, without delaying treatment in suspected sepsis

easy: Young, otherwise healthy adult with a short history of fever, cough, and sore throat
Clear localizing symptom such as dysuria or productive cough
Vital signs stable, no red flags
Fever responds to acetaminophen and the patient looks well
medium: Older adult with fever and confusion but no localizing symptoms
Fever with a new medication started two weeks earlier
Fever with night sweats and weight loss
Fever in a patient with diabetes or chronic kidney disease
hard: Immunocompromised patient with fever but no localizing signs
Fever of unknown origin lasting more than three weeks
Fever with a normal white count and no source found on initial workup
Fever in an infant under three months with nonspecific symptoms
Fever with relative bradycardia suggesting typhoid, Legionella, or drug fever
